Central Nervous System
Physiology
Sleep and memory

Quick Overview

This lesson covers sleep and memory. Sleep is defined and its normal duration given, the two sleep types (slow wave and REM) are compared, and the four theories of sleep and the effects of sleep deprivation are outlined. Memory is then classified into sensory, short-term and long-term stores, with the cellular mechanisms behind immediate, short-term and long-term memory.

Sleep

Definition and duration

Sleep is a state of loss of consciousness from which a person can be aroused by normal, non-harmful stimuli.

Normal duration varies with age:

  • Newborn infant: 16–18 hours every 24 hours.
  • Young adult: 7–9 hours every 24 hours.
  • Old persons: fewer hours.

Types of sleep

FeatureSlow wave sleep (SWS)Rapid eye movement sleep (REM)
OccurrenceMost of sleep during the nightIn episodes during the night
Episode lengthAbout 80–90 minutesOnly about 15 minutes
Share of sleep time75%25%
Duration increases whenPerson is very tired (and vice versa)Person has no desire to sleep
Eye movementsNoneVery characteristic rapid eye movements
Cardiovascular / respiratory30% reduction in cardiovascular and metabolic activitiesHeart rate, blood pressure and respiration irregular and may increase
DreamsOccur but are not rememberedActive dreams, remembered
Brain wavesVery slow (delta waves)Like the wakefulness state
ArousalEasier to arouseDifficult to arouse
Muscle toneSlightly inhibited; no abnormal movementsExtreme inhibition due to increased activity of inhibitory supraspinal centers; few irregular movements
Brain activityNot active, diminished metabolismHighly active, increased metabolism (paradoxical sleep)
Genital responseNo penile erectionErection in genital organs even in children, and of the clitoris in females

Theories (mechanisms) of sleep

1. Passive theory

The reticular activating system receives visual, auditory and tactile impulses from the surroundings and activates the cerebral cortex, causing wakefulness. Fatigue of these neural circuits was thought to cause sleep until recovery occurs.

Transection of the brainstem in the mid-pontine region produces a brain that never goes to sleep, indicating other centers below the mid pons send impulses to higher centers to cause sleep.

2. Active theory

Stimulation of certain CNS areas produces sleep: middle raphe nuclei (lower pons and medulla), nucleus of tractus solitarius, rostral part of the hypothalamus, and some diffuse thalamic nuclei. The locus ceruleus is considered the center for REM sleep; its neurons secrete norepinephrine.

3. Metabolic theory

Prolonged wakefulness causes progressive accumulation of chemical substances (such as muramyl peptide and the sleep factor serotonin) in the brainstem and CSF; at a certain concentration they produce sleep.

4. Positive feedback theory

A positive feedback mechanism exists between the reticular formation and the cerebral cortex while the sleeping centers are inactive. It maintains wakefulness until it becomes fatigued or the sleeping centers become active, explaining the periodicity between sleep and wakefulness.

Importance of sleep and effects of deprivation

Sleep restores normal levels of activity and balance among the different parts of CNS neurons. Sleep deprivation:

  • Makes CNS neurons lose their baseline physiological operations.
  • Causes malfunction of the mind and abnormal behavior: irritability, even psychosis, great loss of concentration and extreme fatigability.
  • Increases sympathetic activity all over the body.
  • Disturbs other body functions (digestion, absorption, hormone secretion, vasomotor and cardiovascular regulation), secondary to disturbed nervous control.

Memory

Definition and stores

Memory is the ability to record, retain and retrieve knowledge. There are three types: sensory memory, short-term memory and long-term memory.

Human memory is usefully described as a set of stores (sensory, short-term, long-term), which are "places" to put information, plus a set of processes (encoding, maintenance, retrieval) that act on them. Information passes from sensory memory into short-term memory by attention filtering the stimuli.

General mechanism

  • Memory traces: certain information causes neural activity with changes in synaptic transmission; these traces are activated by the thinking mind to produce the memory. Memory can be integrated at many CNS levels.
  • Negative memory: the basal limbic region determines whether information is important; the brain ignores much information and remembers only one memory at a given moment.

Classification and mechanisms

1. Immediate memory

E.g. remembering a telephone number for a few seconds. Mechanism: reverberating circuit, or presynaptic facilitation (prolonged Ca²⁺ channel opening).

2. Short-term memory

Lasts a few minutes up to days. Mechanism: presynaptic facilitation.

  1. Facilitatory interneurons are stimulated and release serotonin.
  2. Serotonin activates presynaptic receptors, activating adenyl cyclase and increasing cyclic AMP.
  3. Cyclic AMP activates protein kinase, which phosphorylates proteins and blocks K⁺ channels.
  4. K⁺ channel blockage prolongs the presynaptic action potential, so voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels stay active, giving maintained Ca²⁺ influx and transmitter release onto the postsynaptic neurons.

3. Long-term memory

Due to actual structural changes at synapses:

  • Permanent adhesion of synaptic vesicles to the presynaptic membrane.
  • Marked increase in surface area of the presynaptic membrane through which transmitter is released.
  • Increased enzyme and protein synthesis, activating transmitter formation and release.

Key Points / Quick Review

Sleep basics

  • Loss of consciousness, arousable by normal non-harmful stimuli.
  • Newborn 16–18 h; young adult 7–9 h; elderly less.

SWS

  • 75% of sleep; 80–90 min; delta waves; no eye movements.
  • 30% reduction in CV and metabolic activity; dreams not remembered.

REM

  • 25% of sleep; 15 min episodes; wakefulness-like waves; paradoxical sleep.
  • Extreme muscle tone inhibition; irregular HR, BP, respiration; remembered dreams.

Theories of sleep

  • Passive, active, metabolic, positive feedback.
  • Locus ceruleus (norepinephrine) = REM center.

Sleep deprivation

  • Irritability, psychosis, poor concentration, fatigability.
  • Increased sympathetic activity; disturbed autonomic and endocrine functions.

Memory stores

  • Sensory, short-term, long-term; processes: encoding, maintenance, retrieval.
  • Attention filtering moves information from sensory to short-term memory.

Immediate and short-term memory

  • Immediate: reverberating circuit or prolonged Ca²⁺ channel opening.
  • Short-term: serotonin → cAMP → protein kinase → K⁺ channel block → prolonged Ca²⁺ influx.

Long-term memory

  • Permanent vesicle adhesion, larger release surface, more enzyme and protein synthesis.
